summary: Cheapest price from src to dst with at most k stops (k + 1 edges).
mainInsight: Bellman-Ford limited to k + 1 rounds: in each round relax every flight using a copy of the previous round's distances, so a path never uses more edges than the number of rounds. Dijkstra needs (node, stops) states because the cheapest path to a node may use too many stops.

approaches.name: Bellman-Ford for k + 1 rounds
approaches.summary: Relax all edges k + 1 times from a copied array.

approaches.name: BFS / Dijkstra on (node, stops)
approaches.summary: Track the cost and the stops used.

commonMistakes: Updating the distance array in place
Using k rounds instead of k + 1
Using plain Dijkstra with a visited set

promptVariants: Why does the stop constraint break plain Dijkstra?
options: The cheapest path may use too many stops, so stops must be in the state
Dijkstra cannot handle directed graphs with cycles at all
Flight prices may be negative, which Dijkstra forbids
The graph may contain parallel edges between two cities
cards.answer: The cheapest path may use too many stops, so stops must be in the state
cards.explanation: A pricier path with fewer stops can be the only feasible one.

promptVariants: Why must Bellman-Ford copy the distance array each round?
What goes wrong if you update in place?
cards.answer: Round i must only extend paths found in round i - 1. Updating the same array in place lets an update in round i feed another edge in the same round, effectively using more than i edges and violating the k stops limit.
keyPoints: Round i = paths with at most i edges
Use a copy of the previous distances
